Canonical Sufficiency
kan-ON-ih-kul suh-FISH-en-see
noun phrase (theological doctrine)
From Late Latin canonicus (of the canon, from canon; see Closed Canon) + Latin sufficientia (adequacy, from sufficere, to be adequate or enough, from sub- under + facere, to do). The doctrine names the positive content of sola Scriptura: the canonical Scriptures are sufficient — not supplemented, not supplanted — for every matter of faith, worship, and godly life.

Biblical Definition

Canonical sufficiency is the doctrine that the sixty-six books of Scripture provide everything necessary for the knowledge of God, the way of salvation, and the ordering of Christian life — without supplement from tradition, reason, experience, or additional revelation. The classic proof text is 2 Timothy 3:16–17: the God-breathed Scriptures make the man of God “complete” (artios) and “equipped for every good work” (exartizo) — fully furnished, not partially supplied. The two Greek verbs are emphatic: artios means fitted out, ready; the compound exartizo adds the prefix ex- to intensify: completely, thoroughly equipped. What is thoroughly equipping the man of God for every good work requires no supplement. Peter’s claim is equally comprehensive: God’s divine power “According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue:” (2 Pet. 1:3) — not some things, not most things, but all things pertaining to the believer’s life and piety. Deuteronomy 29:29 marks the limit: “the secret things belong to the LORD our God, but those things which are revealed belong to us and to our children.” Scripture is sufficient because God has revealed everything He intends us to know; the secret things He withholds are not accessible through tradition or experience either. The 1689 Baptist Confession (1:6) states it directly: the whole counsel of God “concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man’s salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down or necessarily contained therein.”

Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that the sixty-six books of the biblical canon are fully adequate — sufficient without supplement from tradition, psychology, or new revelation — for all knowledge of salvation, faith, worship, and godly life; the positive content of sola Scriptura.

CANONICAL SUFFICIENCY, n. (Theology) The Reformed doctrine that the inspired canonical Scriptures are fully adequate — sufficient without supplement from magisterium, tradition, modern prophecy, or secular psychology — for all matters of faith, salvation, worship, and the ordering of Christian life. The positive content of sola Scriptura.

2. Opposed to (a) Rome’s co-authority of Scripture and Tradition (Trent: both to be received “with equal piety and reverence”); (b) the charismatic claim that Scripture must be supplemented by modern prophecy; (c) the therapeutic model that treats Scripture as spiritually helpful but insufficient for “clinical” pastoral care.

3. Scope: canonical sufficiency does not claim the Bible answers every empirical or scientific question. It claims that for faith, salvation, worship, and the life of godliness, the Word is enough; pastors need not consult psychological literature for the church’s spiritual health — the Word and prayer suffice (Acts 6:4).

4. Confessional basis: Westminster Confession (1:6) and 1689 Baptist Confession (1:6): “The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man’s salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture.”

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

2 Timothy 3:17 — "That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works."

2 Peter 1:3 — "According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue:"

Deuteronomy 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

Modern Corruption

Rome supplements Scripture with Tradition and the Magisterium; therapeutic counseling culture supplements it with psychology; charismatic movements supplement it with prophecy — each substituting human additions for the self-sufficient Word that Paul declares makes the man of God “complete.”

expand to see more

Rome’s Council of Trent formally established a two-source theory of divine revelation: Scripture and unwritten apostolic traditions are to be received “with equal veneration.” Vatican II refined this but did not revoke it; the practical result is that the Magisterium — the bishops in union with the pope — functions as the authoritative interpreter of both Scripture and Tradition, a third source over the other two. Against this, the Reformation confessions are categorical: Scripture and Scripture alone is the supreme judge in all religious controversies (1689 Baptist Confession, 1:10). No tradition, however ancient, and no council, however learned, binds the conscience apart from Scripture; each must be tested by it.

Within the evangelical world, canonical sufficiency is eroded in two contemporary directions. First, the integration of secular psychology into pastoral counseling treats the biblical categories of sin, repentance, and sanctification as spiritually helpful but clinically insufficient, positioning the therapist’s couch as a supplement the Word does not supply. Second, the pursuit of “fresh words from God” in charismatic worship treats the written Word as a cold text needing warming by subjective experience and prophetic additions. Both errors contradict Paul’s claim in 2 Timothy 3:16–17: all Scripture, as written, is sufficient to make the minister of God complete — not a starting point to supplement but a complete deposit to preach.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin canonicus (of the rule, the standard list) + sufficere (to be enough); the doctrine names the self-sufficiency of the canon — it needs no propping by tradition, emotion, or additional revelation because what God breathed out is by definition adequate for the purpose He gave it.

expand to see more

Latin sufficere — to be enough, from sub- (up from under) + facere (to make, do); what is “sufficient” undergirds the whole from beneath without needing support from outside — the canon supports the church, the church does not support the canon

Greek artios — complete, fully fit for purpose (2 Tim. 3:17); the Word makes the believer artios — not partially equipped but fully outfitted for every good work

Greek exartizo — to equip completely, furnish thoroughly; the prefix ex- (completely, out) intensifies artizo — the equipping that Scripture provides is total, leaving no gap that tradition or psychology must fill

Latin totus — whole, entire; canonical sufficiency concerns the tota canon as a whole — no single proof text bears all the weight; the sufficiency is the sufficiency of the sixty-six books taken together

Greek theopneustos — God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16); what God breathes out is by definition sufficient — it is His own Word, not a partial disclosure requiring human supplements to be complete

Usage

"Canonical sufficiency is the Reformed answer to “where do we go for authoritative guidance?” — the answer is Scripture alone, not Scripture plus tradition, plus the Magisterium, plus modern prophecy, plus therapeutic insights that allegedly go where the Bible does not reach."

"When pastors or counselors treat secular psychology as a necessary supplement to biblical categories for pastoral care, they deny canonical sufficiency in practice even if they affirm it confessionally — effectively saying Paul’s “complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim. 3:17) falls short of clinical competence."

"The doctrine protects the preacher: his task is to preach the Word (2 Tim. 4:2), not to supplement it — because it already contains everything necessary, and his calling is to unfold what is there, not to add what he imagines is missing."
